content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for reviewing our paper! Here are two responses to the weaknesses that you have pointed out, can you please let us know if this additional information improves your perspective on the paper?

> When comparing the time of algorithms, the time of Meta OT should include the training time. 

Appendix C.3 of our paper reports the training time for the MNIST and Spherical examples and shows that those models take less than 10 minutes (~10-20k iterations) to train on our Quadro GP100 GPU to reach the optimal predictions on the training sets.

> This paper does not explain why meta can help to quickly predict and solve new problems by using knowledge and information from past problems

The information from the past OT problems comes up in the loss (e.g., eq. 16) of how we train the predictive model. The model predicts a solution to the problems and the parameters are updated to better-optimize the OT problem (in alg. 3). Thus as the training progresses in alg. 3, the information from the earlier OT problems is used to help predict the solution to new problems that are sampled.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
In section 2, the authors recall the OT dual formulation in the case of $W_2$ distance and the entropic OT. Based on simpler formulas of computing OT cost for those cases, they proposed  to use neural network to  modeling the cost function. Section 4 includes experiments of discrete OT on MNIST data, transportation on spherical data and colour transfers using Wasserstein-2 distance. The results show that the meta OT needs significant less number of iterations to converge than the Sinkhorn algorithm.  In the last section, the authors claim the contribution and outline limitations of their methods.

Overall, I think the idea is simple and interesting. I am concerned about the novelty of the method as well as its non-applicability in many important situations  as the authors have stated. The authors also do not show the amount of  time  to build up their meta-OT. It is very important issue because if the number of supports of a discrete distribution is extremely large, then  the main questions are how long does it take to train the meta-OT and can we guarantee the accuracy of its solution? 

To improve the paper, the authors might try to include some approximation theory to quantify the solution's  accuracy and show why the Meta-OT initialisation improve the convergence speed of Sinkhorn algorithm.

Thank you very much for the review! We have written a separate response on the potential applications we see for Meta OT methods. Can you please review that and consider it for your final evaluation of our paper? Here are inline responses to your other questions and comments:

> I would have like to see more systematic analysis of the decay of performance associated with different degrees of out-of-distribution problems, as well as with greater or less coherence within the domain of generalization.

Appendix D shows out-of-distribution generalization when predicting the optimal couplings between image datasets, is this a first step towards the analysis you would like to see? One nice property we like about the Meta OT setting is that *generalization issues are detectable* in practice. In other words, if the model makes a bad prediction, then we can check the optimality conditions for the OT problem it is trying to solve (such as the marginal error or dual objectives our paper reports) and discard the prediction and re-solve the problem from scratch if it does not result in an acceptable solution. We are especially optimistic in discrete settings because they are convex optimization problems that Sinkhorn is capable of converging on from *any* initialization.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a meta-learning approach to OT. That is, the authors learn a meta-model on a large train set of OT tasks and then try to predict the solution of the new test OT tasks based on the past experience. Two experimental setups are considered: discrete OT problems for general costs and continuous (small-dimensional) OT problems for the quadratic cost. In both cases, the authors state that the meta-ot predictions notably speed up the OT learning algorithms (meta-prediction is used as the initialization in the OT algorithm). The performance is demonstrated on 2D, 3D optimal transport tasks: interpolation between MNIST digits (considered as 2D distributions), supply-demand transportation and color transfer between RGB images (represented as 3D point clouds).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity, quality.** First, from the exposition, it is not clear to which extent meta-OT is actually capable of predicting the reasonably precise solutions of OT problems or it anyway requires fine-tuning. I think this aspect should be discussed in a more detail. 

* In the supply-demand example, Figure 5 is an awesome picture, but it explains literally nothing. Is it a good initial (meta-OT) plan? Is its cost already close to the optimal (entropic) one?
* In most cases, the authors provide some convergence plots of the dual objective and show the marginal error. It would be nice to see the marginal values immediately after Meta-OT prediction (before further fine-tuning) for comparison. Additionally, I would expect to see the transport cost (entropic, a.k.a. The primal objective) of the recovered plan at all these stages. This would help to understand further potential of the method.
* In section 4.3, the provided examples are images but it unfortunately remains unclear what happens inside their color palettes (where the transport magic actually happens). How good is the recovered transport (both meta-OT prediction and meta+finetune) between the palettes? I think it is useful to add some examples with the color palettes – otherwise the experiment is not transparent. I am concerned here because such problems can be solved reasonably well by much simpler methods without ANY learning or meta-learning. For example, just by aligning means and stds of RGB channels (like AdaIN used in style transfer) or just by Gaussian (linear OT ot.da.OT_mapping_linear ). This won’t guarantee the correct measure transport, but would in most cases anyway result in good image color transfer qualitatively. Is there any benefit in using (rather complicated) meta-OT here?

Second, after reading the paper twice, I feel that I do not completely understand what are the scenarios where we need to solve OT repeatedly, so where the proposed methodology is actually applicable. I found only one-two sentences in the text describing this rather important aspect (paragraph 3 in introduction) and only very briefly. I kindly ask the authors to provide a more explicit description of a particular use-cases of their methodology. For example, regarding the supply-demand example, do the trading companies really need to solve the OT problem so frequently that it is required to reduce the computation amount? Shouldn’t they, for example, plan once a month or so? This does not seem to be a scenario requiring meta-OT. I am definitely not expert in logistics/trading, but just trying to understand this (rather important for the current paper) motivational aspect.

**Novelty.** The paper limited scientific novelty – it is just an application of Meta Learning principles to a field which has not been meta learned before (optimal transport). Regarding the methodological/technical novelty, there are some clever methodological ideas, e.g., predicting the dual variables rather than the OT plan, but I can not say these are very significant as almost any (non-meta) OT algorithm (either discrete or continuous) anyway solves the dual problem rather than the primal.

**Reproducibility:** the code is present – no questions here.

**Other**
* Notation overline(psi) for the parameters of the neural network is a little bit weird.
* Most paper seems to be using the amortized optimization (14). Have you tried the regression-based approach (15)?
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper has limited scientific novelty – it is a application of Meta Learning to OT which is rather straightforward and its significance is not clear. On the one hand, it seems to indeed boost the underlying OT algorithms thanks to the good predicted initialization of dual variables and overall it is interesting to see that OT problems can be (to some extent) meta-learned. On the other hand, the potential applications prospect of Meta-OT are not convincing enough (do we really need to meta-learn OT?) and there are some questions in the experiments. I currently rate this paper as a borderline, and will wait for the authors feedback to make my final decision.

**Post-rebuttal update:** score +1 (see the discussion under the general authors comment)

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for the review and the insightful questions! We have written a separate response on the potential applications we see for Meta OT methods. Can you please review that and consider it for your final evaluation of our paper? Here are inline responses to your other questions and comments:

> In the supply-demand example, Figure 5 is an awesome picture, but it explains literally nothing. Is it a good initial (meta-OT) plan? Is its cost already close to the optimal (entropic) one? [...] It would be nice to see the marginal values immediately after Meta-OT prediction (before further fine-tuning) for comparison.

We think the figure provides a nice qualitative visualization for 1) how close the Meta OT’s prediction is to the ground-truth and 2) the significant variation between the different OT problems we consider. Figure 4 above this offers quantitative results to answer your questions by measuring the marginal error, which is the standard way of assessing the quality of approximate transport maps and is almost always used as a convergence criterion for Sinkhorn solvers. The marginal error of the initial prediction is shown at iteration 0 on the right side of Figure 4. It is approximately 10-20% better than the sinkhorn initialization and results in significantly faster convergence to more accurate solutions after fine-tuning it with sinkhorn.

> (3) The capabilities of the method are only to predict good initialization for sinkhorn/W2GN, but not the good approximation of the OT plan (not sure here);

The predicted duals are good approximations to the OT plan. The initializations of the dual variables for sinkhorn/W2GN can directly be used to recover the OT plan and the connections here are well-known. We present how to do this in the discrete case in eq. (6) and in the continuous case in eq. (11).

> How good is the recovered transport (both meta-OT prediction and meta+finetune) between the palettes?

Figure 7 estimates the dual objective of the prediction and compares it to a random initialization. This is the standard way of quantifying the quality of the OT solution and shows that the prediction is extremely close to the optimal dual value found by running W2GN.

> For example, regarding the supply-demand example, do the trading companies really need to solve the OT problem so frequently that it is required to reduce the computation amount? Shouldn’t they, for example, plan once a month or so? This does not seem to be a scenario requiring meta-OT. I am definitely not expert in logistics/trading, but just trying to understand this (rather important for the current paper) motivational aspect.

We agree it's not useful to improve a computation that is only run once every month, but there are variations on this where Meta OT would be extremely helpful. One of them is if the trading company wishes to use the OT as a loss to evaluate the design of new components or variations of their infrastructure. Then, searching over the design space would require simulating many related OT problems to evaluate every new design and Meta OT methods would be great at avoiding redundant computations arising here.

> Notation overline(psi) for the parameters of the neural network is a little bit weird.

We agree, we used it to stay consistent with the notation in the W2GN paper.

>  Most paper seems to be using the amortized optimization (14). Have you tried the regression-based approach (15)?

We prototyped it at the beginning of the project and found it worked reasonably well. We didn't like that it required the ground-truth solutions to the OT problems that can be computationally expensive and instead decided to focus on the objective-based approach. It would make sense to explore in settings where high-quality solutions are already available so we decided to keep this part in the text.

display_title: Applicability of Meta OT and related work

content.title: Applicability of Meta OT and related work
content.comment:
While the reviewers seem to be in consensus that Meta OT is conceptually appealing and a reasonable way of combining meta-learning, amortized optimization, and OT, their main concern is on the applicability, stating:
+ “*the potential applications of the Meta-OT methodology are questionable*” [zFaG]
+ “*the specific problem, in which one is solving structurally related problems repeatedly, is a bit niche*” [eM4a]
+ “*I am concerned about the novelty of the method as well as its non-applicability in many important situations*” [HF6W].

For the final evaluation of our paper, we kindly ask the reviewers and AC to consider the following settings. We will also update the paper with this context. There is a clear trend towards repeatedly solving OT in ML, science, and engineering applications. In ML settings, for example, this happens when optimal transport is used as part of the model or the loss. There is a large potential for Meta OT formulations to help improve these settings that are otherwise bottlenecked by needing to solve the OT problem from scratch to evaluate the model every time it changes. Here are three key areas of related works:

## Other settings repeatedly solving optimal transport problems.

There have been a few papers posted concurrently to ours that also investigate repeatedly solving OT problems. We think the formulations we have chosen to study, i.e., objective-based amortization for MLPs and hyper-networks in discrete and continuous settings, offers an interesting perspective for practitioners to consider in addition to these other papers:
+ Published at NeurIPS 2022 this year, [Supervised Training of Conditional Monge Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.14262) by Bunne et al. investigate repeatedly solving OT problems in continuous settings in biological settings to infer the effects of treatments on cells. This is crucial as a new OT problem needs to be solved to analyze the treatment effect and there are clear learnable structures between information such as the type of treatment and patient information and how it impacts the cells. The submitted version of our paper includes a perspective in the appendix of how their conditional model can be seen as a conditional process while the Meta ICNN we investigated can be seen as a hyper-network. One point our paper adds is that the amortized model’s prediction can be rapidly fine-tuned.
+ [GeONet: a neural operator for learning the Wasserstein geodesic](https://openreview.net/forum?id=cuZNcYohQCX) is a concurrent submission to this ICLR that is also motivated by repeatedly solving OT problems in continuous settings via the Benamou-Brenier dynamic OT formulation, which is a PDE. In contrast to our methods, they focus on learning a neural operator that “amortizes” the solutions to the PDE given additional information about the measures.

## Optimal transport as a loss

This is another crucial setting where OT problems are repeatedly solved to find the parameters of a model or of one of the measures:
+ In the physical sciences, this is especially interesting for solving inverse imaging problems where physical properties are measured, e.g. with radar, and then the parameters of a model are learned using as OT loss to result in measurements that are the closest to the observed ones. Two starting references, among many others, for this are  [Seismic Imaging and Optimal Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.04801) and [Application of optimal transport and the quadratic Wasserstein metric to full-waveform inversion](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10090161).
+ OT losses are also budding for ML and computer vision applications where OT problems are repeatedly solved to evaluate the loss as the model changes. A few starting references for this large topic are: [DeepEMD: Few-Shot Image Classification With Differentiable Earth Mover's Distance and Structured Classifiers](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_CVPR_2020/papers/Zhang_DeepEMD_Few-Shot_Image_Classification_With_Differentiable_Earth_Movers_Distance_and_CVPR_2020_paper.pdf),  [Differential Properties of Sinkhorn Approximation for Learning with Wasserstein Distance](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11897), and [A Unified Framework for Implicit Sinkhorn Differentiation](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2022/papers/Eisenberger_A_Unified_Framework_for_Implicit_Sinkhorn_Differentiation_CVPR_2022_paper.pdf).

## Optimal transport for gradient flows
Gradient flows are often numerically estimated using the celebrated Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme, which involves repeatedly solving many OT subproblems that the standard methods solve from scratch every time. Meta OT thus also has the potential to drastically improve JKO computations. Two starting references for these are [Optimizing Functionals on the Space of Probabilities with Input Convex Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.00774) and
[Proximal Optimal Transport Modeling of Population Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.06345).

content.title: Response to the authors
content.comment:
Dear authors, thanks for your answers! After reading the answers, I still think that meta OT lacks a killer application. I am rather confident here because I see that the other reviewers also raise analogous concerns in their reviews. Here are my thoughts regarding the feedback:
- I agree that the application of Bunne et al. (**conditional OT**) may be relevant for meta-OT. Is it possible to perform comparison with Bunne et al. in some (continuous) setup? Is there an example which clearly demonstrates the advantages of meta-OT w.r.t. the conditional OT?
- I do not understand why using Meta OT as the **loss** is reasonable. In this case, each particular learning scenario may be very specific and it is not obvious how to cover it with "meta-distribution". It seems easier to just pick the fitted OT from the previous model step as the initialization for the current step and then fine-tune it (rather than predict from scratch). I think the same can be applied to the gradient flows case.

My opinion is that at least toy proof-of-concept experiments here are needed as the provided examples are still not convincing. It would be great if the authors could provide them during the remaining time.

replying_to: Replying to Response to the authors

content.title: Response
content.comment:
> I agree that the application of Bunne et al. (conditional OT) may be relevant for meta-OT. Is it possible to perform comparison with Bunne et al. in some (continuous) setup? Is there an example which clearly demonstrates the advantages of meta-OT w.r.t. the conditional OT?

Both the conditional OT paper and ours have settings that predict solutions to Euclidean Wasserstein-2 transport problems. Conditional OT methods focus on a predicting the solutions with a PICNN, similar to a conditional neural process, and we have proposed to instead use a hypernetwork. Both approaches seem worth considering when predicting solutions to OT problems, but we are unfortunately not sure what the right concrete comparison would be. We also apologize if the positioning of our paper is confusing with respect to the conditional OT paper as we independently developed many of the ideas earlier this year before their paper was released. We are open to re-positioning and better-contextualizing our paper with respect to the conditional OT paper if there are any concrete suggestions here: the hypernetwork we consider could be used in their setting and the PICNN they consider could be used in ours.

The easiest comparison we could add is to use the conditional OT's PICNN approach in our continuous color transfer setting. However, if you already do not think that the color transfer setting is interesting, then it seems unlikely that our ablation re-implementing the PICNN-based approach would be helpful. The other comparison would be to try to evaluate a hypernetwork-based approach in the conditional OT experimental settings for predicting drug effects. However to the best of our knowledge, there is no easy way to reproducing the conditional OT experimental results. (Maybe they will open-source it soon?)

>  I do not understand why using Meta OT as the loss is reasonable. In this case, each particular learning scenario may be very specific and it is not obvious how to cover it with "meta-distribution". It seems easier to just pick the fitted OT from the previous model step as the initialization for the current step and then fine-tune it (rather than predict from scratch). I think the same can be applied to the gradient flows case.

We agree there are settings where using OT as a loss can use the previous solution to start the current solver and that Meta OT predictions wouldn't help. Wasserstein GANs are also a good example of this where the potentials estimating the Wasserstein-1 distance are continually updated alongside the generator.

The repeated solves where Meta OT would be helpful is when each instance in the batch requires solving an OT problem, which arises exactly in the settings considered by the CVPR 2022 paper [A Unified Framework for Implicit Sinkhorn Differentiation](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2022/papers/Eisenberger_A_Unified_Framework_for_Implicit_Sinkhorn_Differentiation_CVPR_2022_paper.pdf). [Here](https://github.com/marvin-eisenberger/implicit-sinkhorn/blob/main/sinkhorn/sinkhorn.py#L33) is the implementation for their Sinkhorn solver showing that it always starts from scratch. This is a Meta OT setting that would undoubtedly benefit from predictions of the initializations when being deployed. We think the demonstrations we've provided should be a sufficient starting point for anybody wishing to do this.

> My opinion is that at least toy proof-of-concept experiments here are needed as the provided examples are still not convincing. It would be great if the authors could provide them during the remaining time.

We think that our existing experimental demonstrations already show proof-of-concept experiments in predicting the solutions to discrete and Euclidean Wasserstein-2 OT problems and are not sure that more toy proof-of-concept experiments would better-help disseminate the core ideas in here, unless you have another extremely concrete suggestion. At this point, we do not think that adding more experimental results during the rest of the ICLR review process would be scientifically healthy as there is not enough time for us to ensure that we properly execute the ideas and not enough time for you and the other reviewers to properly confirm they are valid. (We also thought the reviewer-author discussion was closing yesterday.)

content.title: Further discussion
content.comment:
Dear authors,

- After the rebuttal for me it became clear that meta-OT and conditional-OT target at rougly the same scope of applications. Your position on impossibility of comparison with conditional-OT of Bunne et al. (*in their setup*) is understandable and I accept it. I also agree that the color transfer or MNIST (*your setup*) is not the best application to compare. Nevertheless, since the authors anyway consider these applications, it seems reasonable to at least demonstrate how the competitive conditional-OT works in these setups. I also note that it is possible to do quantitative comparison, e.g., by comparing the values of the dual objectives of both methods.

**Related comment:** in the color transfer, it would be nice to qualitatively see how close is the initial predicted point cloud by meta-OT to the ground truth. I have already pointed in my initial review that just demonstrating the final "transfered" images in not enough and the color palletes should be added as well. This will make the qualitative elaluation more transparent (what happens in the actual space of disctibutions on 3D where meta-OT magic wand works?). 

- I do not accept the claim that meta-OT could be useful for OT loss applications. All the experiments in the current paper consider *static* setups, i.e., when the input-target distributions pairs are samples from some meta-distribution which one may at least describe how it looks like. In the *dynamic* setup (OT loss), one distribution comes from this *static* meta distribution, while the other one is always changing following the gradient flow (starting from some initial distribution) w.r.t. OT loss. It is not obvious how to precisely describe such meta distributions whether meta-OT could work in this *dynamic* case.

Following the discussion and some clarifications from the authors, I raise my score for this paper a little bit (by 1). However, I still think this a borderline paper and could benefit from a more transparent discussion and comparision with Bunne et al. One of the key issues for me it is not clear is meta-OT better/worse than conditional OT.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
>  Related comment: in the color transfer, it would be nice to qualitatively see how close is the initial predicted point cloud by meta-OT to the ground truth. I have already pointed in my initial review that just demonstrating the final "transfered" images in not enough and the color palletes should be added as well.

Do you mean qualitative or quantitative here? If it's qualitative, then we are showing the initial predictions from the model (and not the final fine-tuned versions (in figure 6 and the appendix). If quantitative, then we are showing the dual objectives of the predictions as they are fine-tuned (in figure 7) in comparison to running W2GN from the default initialization. This is a standard way of comparing the quality of OT solutions and we didn't want to specialize too much to the color transfer setting, but we can also add in some other quantitative evaluations, such as other image similarity metrics or comparisons between the color palettes.

>  I do not accept the claim that meta-OT could be useful for OT loss applications. [and static vs dynamic settings] 

We agree that using Meta OT for the loss (or model) has the additional moving part where one of the meta distributions is changing during training, i.e., it is dynamic, in contrast to the static/fixed meta distributions we consider in the paper. While the static distributions provide a much cleaner testbed for evaluating and comparing the meta OT part in isolation, we are optimistic about extensions into dynamic settings as many other settings successfully amortize in these dynamic settings: 1) amortized variational inference (and VAEs) are successfully able to predict the maximum of the variational posterior throughout training as the decoder changes the distribution, and 2) RL policy learning is successfully able to amortize the Q function learning throughout training as the Q function is also updated during training (References for these are in sections 6.1 and 6.6 of [the amortized optimization tutorial](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00665)).  While these may not have accurate predictions during training because the problems are changing, amortization is still crucial for rapidly training and result in reasonable predictions by the end of training when deploying after everything has converged. The key amortization components in these dynamic settings is simply an application of the ideas from the static settings.

> Following the discussion and some clarifications from the authors, I raise my score for this paper a little bit (by 1). However, I still think this a borderline paper and could benefit from a more transparent discussion and comparision with Bunne et al.

While this would be a drastic change to the positioning of our paper, we are very open to renaming our paper to "*On warm-starting for conditional optimal transport*" to 1) unify the terminology "Meta OT" and "conditional OT" on the same concept. We would replace the term "Meta OT" in our paper with "conditional OT" everywhere; and 2) emphasize the fact that we investigate the use of warm-starting with the model's prediction to improve the solution to the OT problems. This was not considered in the conditional OT paper (partially because in some settings they assume to *only* have access to the conditional information and not full information about the measures). These updates should also help change the focus from the modeling part (where either a hypernetwork or a neural process could be used) to the fact that these models can be fine-tuned with the original OT problem. We can also emphasize that we investigate discrete/Sinkhorn settings that were also not considered in the conditional OT paper.  We originally did not consider presenting our paper like this because we developed Meta OT earlier this year concurrent to the conditional OT paper and were not aware of it until recently.

Would these updates further improve your perspective on our contribution? It looks like OpenReview is not permitting us to upload a new version of the paper, but we are fully committed to continuing this discussion and properly integrating any final changes we agree on into the final version of the paper. We are also open to hearing from the perspective from the other reviewers and AC.

display_title: New paper on predicting Sinkhorn initializations and suitability for TMLR?

content.title: New paper on predicting Sinkhorn initializations and suitability for TMLR?
content.comment:
Dear reviewers and AC,

We still feel that the idea of predicting solutions to optimal transport problems with Meta OT is a timely idea that is worth presenting at this ICLR and argue that our paper presents demonstrations and benchmarks that future papers in this space will be able to build on and refer to. To the best of our knowledge and predictive capabilities, the reviewers and AC are currently leaning towards rejecting this paper because they are not convinced that there will be enough applications of the idea. In addition to the [GeONet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.14440) and [conditional OT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.14262) papers presenting very closely related ideas and applications, another paper entitled [Generative Adversarial Learning of Sinkhorn Algorithm Initializations](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.00133.pdf) was posted a few days ago on November 30. This paper directly builds on the Meta OT settings (e.g. entropic OT between MNIST and quick draw) and explores other approaches to predicting the solutions.

We believe that publishing our paper in ICLR will provide a starting point for other Meta OT research to build on and kindly ask that you take this into consideration for your final evaluation of the paper.

If you decide to reject our paper, we will probably submit a near-identical version of the paper to TMLR as the [TMLR guidelines](https://www.jmlr.org/tmlr/editorial-policies.html) clearly state "*formalization of new learning tasks (e.g., in the context of new applications) and of methods for assessing performance on those tasks*" as an acceptance criteria. We believe that learning to predict the solutions of OT problems is a sufficiently new and interesting learning task, even though there are still a significant number of potential new applications that we could explore and modeling/loss methodologies to ablate (including to conditional OT, which was posted *after* we posted the Meta OT paper). We ask the reviewers and AC to comment on whether they would find TMLR a more suitable venue for our paper under these criteria. We will take any concrete suggestions into consideration before re-submitting the paper, and believe your comments would also be useful for any potential future TMLR reviewers reading these threads

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The paper proposes metaOT an amortized optimization method for optimal transport. A meta network predicts the dual variables of the OT problem for pairs of distributions. This method can be used to accelerate solving OT problems that need to be applied  multiple times or to initialize OT solvers. Conceptually the paper is clear and is an  application of meta learning in optimal transport. The authors showed few applications of meta OT in discrete and continuous optimal transport. The discrete ones were more convincing to the reviewers.   

The paper is borderline and was discussed at length between authors reviewers and AC. The main weakness pointed out by the reviewers is regarding the lack of  convincing  applications were metaOT would shine. 

Authors explained in the rebuttal were they can see this used and reviewers and AC suggested few applications. 

We encourage the authors to add one of the suggested applications to their manuscript as it will complete and improve the impact of the work.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The lack of a convincing application of the proposed method.
